info.bio:
Daniel Johnston nació en 1961 en Sacramento (California) y murió el 10 de septiembre de 2019. Es el menor de los 5 hijos de una familia muy cristiana. Empezó a dibujar a una edad muy temprana, mucho antes de iniciarse en la música. Le gustaban músicos como John Lennon, Yoko Ono, Bob Dylan, Elvis Costello, Queen, Neil Young, Sex Pistols y sobretodo los Beatles. “Cuando tenía 19 años, quería ser un Beatle” reconocía Johnston.

De adolescente

scenes.name: Cantautores de los ochenta
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Absorbida la new wave, el mundo de los cantautores no vuelve a ser el mismo: los referentes pasan a ser Dylan, Neil Young, Cohen, Tim Buckley y Joni Mitchell. Las mujeres recuperan su estatus de seres filosóficos: Phranc, Suzanne Vega, Tracy Chapman, Melissa Etheridge, Michelle Shocked, Barbara Manning, Lucinda y Victoria Williams, Indigo Girls y, en Canadá, Jane Siberry, Mary Margaret O'Hara y Sarah McLachlan. Excéntricos: Jandek, Daniel Johnston, David Thomas, Alejandro Escovedo; en California, Stan Ridgway, Chris Isaak y Smog. En Gran Bretaña, Billy Bragg, Robyn Hitchcock, Julian Cope y, la voz más importante de la década, Nick Cave, predicador del apocalipsis moral (From Her To Eternity, The Good Son). Sinéad O'Connor, Sting, Morrissey, Momus; el pop celta de Enya y Loreena McKennitt; al cambiar la década, Joe Henry, Daniel Lanois y Bob Mould.

podcast.title: Kurt Cobain's Influence
podcast.body: Interest in Daniel Johnston's music "spiked" significantly after Kurt Cobain was frequently spotted wearing a Daniel Johnston t-shirt. This public endorsement brought his music global attention and led to reviews around the world. "Then along came Kurt Cobain, who was frequently spotted wearing a Daniel Johnson t-shirt."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Lo-Fi Distribution and Cult Status (1980s)
podcast.body: Daniel Johnston, who suffered from bipolar disorder and frequently visited psychiatric institutions, recorded his songs at home using a $59 Sanyo tape machine propped on his parents' piano. Lacking a way to copy tapes, he would re-perform songs for each copy. He distributed these cassettes while working at McDonald's in Austin, Texas, by dropping them into Big Mac bags, or by giving/selling them to people on the street, which helped him become a local cult favorite due to the honest, childlike, and deeply moving nature of his music. "Tape by tape. McDonald's bag by McDonald's bag, Daniel became a local cult favorite."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mental Illness and Early Career
podcast.body: Daniel Johnston has openly dealt with manic depression and schizophrenia, experiencing "buds of delusion" that raised genuine fears for his safety and that of others. He began his recording career by making cassettes on a $59 Stenial Boombox and gained attention by distributing them to everyone he met under his self-operated label, Stress. "Like Wesley Willis, Daniel has said to deal with mental illness. Manic depression and schizophrenia."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mention in Outsider Music History
podcast.body: Daniel Johnson is listed among artists previously covered as examples of outsider music, alongside Wesley Willis, The Shags, and others. "On those programs, I covered Wesley Willis, the Shags, the legendary Stardust cowboy, Jandic, Captain B. Fart, Daniel Johnson, Florence Foster Jenkins, and even Charles Manson."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Multifaceted Artistic Endeavors
podcast.body: In addition to his music, Daniel Johnston is also an accomplished painter, has helped develop an iPhone game titled "Hi, How Are You?", and has been the subject of multiple documentaries. These diverse artistic contributions showcase his expansive creative talents beyond songwriting. "And not only does he make music, but Daniel also paints. He's helped develop a game for the iPhone called Hi, How Are You? And he's been the subject of a number of documentaries."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Outsider Music Figure and Mainstream Recognition (Early 1990s)
podcast.body: Throughout the 1980s, Daniel Johnston released records that cemented his status as a low-fi hero and an important figure in "outsider music," a genre characterized by technically imperfect but passionately delivered performances. His unique approach and growing underground reputation eventually led to an MTV report on local music scenes. His fame significantly expanded in the early 1990s when Kurt Cobain was seen publicly wearing a Daniel Johnston T-shirt, elevating him to a major cult figure. "And in the early 1990s, when Kurt Cobain was spotted wearing a Daniel Johnston T-shirt, he became a major cult figure."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Professional Recording and Worsening Health
podcast.body: By 1988, Daniel Johnston was well-regarded enough to record professionally in New York, but concurrently, his mental health deteriorated significantly. A notable incident involved him becoming convinced that "Casper, the friendly ghost," had stolen a plane key during a flight with his pilot father, leading to a crash landing and his subsequent commitment. "By 1988, he was well regarded enough to be given a shot of recording professionally in New York. At the same time though, his mental health got worse."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Refusal of Electra Deal
podcast.body: Daniel Johnston famously refused a major record deal from Electra, explaining his decision by stating that Metallica, who were signed to Electra, were "obviously possessed by Satan." He also fired his manager who brought the deal, believing the manager was "obviously possessed too," demonstrating his unique worldview impacting his career choices. "Electra came calling with a major deal, but Daniel refused to sign. Why? Well, because Metallica was on Electra and they were obviously possessed by Satan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Discovery of Daniel Johnston (Early 1990s)
xref.body: After attending a Sonic Youth show in Buffalo, New York, Lou Barlow had a revelation when he heard Daniel Johnston's music playing on a boom box. He immediately recognized it as the kind of music he was already making using a couple of tape decks he had purchased from Radio Shack, solidifying his understanding and appreciation for the lo-fi aesthetic. "Lou Barlow went to a Sonic Youth Show in Buffalo, New York, and after the show, he heard some of Daniel Johnston's music playing on a boom box."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
